title: Reference Angles and Signs by Quadrant
short: Find values in any quadrant from a reference angle and a sign.
trouble: Students use the right value with the wrong sign, such as cos 120° = +1/2.

blocks.html: You know the exact values in the first quadrant. Every other point on the unit circle is a mirror image of a first-quadrant point, so those few values cover the whole circle. You only need to know which mirror, and what it does to the signs.

The reference angle of $\theta$ is the acute angle between its terminal side and the $x$-axis. The trig values of $\theta$ have the same size as those of the reference angle; the quadrant decides the sign.

Reflecting a point across the $y$-axis or the $x$-axis (or both) changes the signs of its coordinates but never their sizes. For example, $150^\circ$ is the mirror image of $30^\circ$ across the $y$-axis, so its point is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$: same numbers, but $x$ is now negative.

blocks.cap: For $\theta$ between $0$ and one full turn. Signs follow from $x$ and $y$: cosine has the sign of $x$, sine the sign of $y$.

blocks.name: unitcircle

opts.task: Turn to $210^\circ$. Its reference angle matches $150^\circ$; what changes?

blocks.cap: The dotted arc is the reference angle. The signs of $(\cos, \sin)$ are printed in each quadrant.

blocks.title: Quadrant II
steps: $120^\circ$ is in Quadrant II. Its reference angle is $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
In Quadrant II, $x < 0$, so cosine is negative.

blocks.title: Quadrant IV, in radians
steps: $\frac{7\pi}{4}$ is just short of $2\pi$, in Quadrant IV. Reference angle: $2\pi - \frac{7\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
In Quadrant IV, $y < 0 < x$, so $\tan = \frac{y}{x}$ is negative.

blocks.title: A negative angle
steps: Add $2\pi$: $-\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is coterminal with $\frac{7\pi}{6}$, in Quadrant III.
In Quadrant III, $y < 0$, so sine is negative.

blocks.html: Using the right size with the wrong sign, such as $\cos 120^\circ = +\frac{1}{2}$. Before you write the answer, picture the terminal side: $120^\circ$ points up and to the left, so its $x$-coordinate, the cosine, must be negative.
